title: The Arabic script and calligraphy
summary: Arabic is written from right to left with 28 letters that join together, and the same script also serves Persian, Urdu and other languages. Over the centuries writing became an art, خَطّ, seen in books and on buildings, tiles and coins. You also meet the Arabic digits and find out why 0–9 are called 'Arabic numerals'.

hero.alt: Arabic calligraphy practice in brown ink on white paper, with reed pens and a small open jar of ink
hero.caption: A student's practice sheet, with reed pens and ink.

sections.title: Right to left: one script, many languages
body: Arabic is written and read from right to left: مِنَ الْيَمِينِ إِلَى الْيَسَار. So an Arabic book opens from what an English reader would call the back. The alphabet has 28 letters, and each letter is a حَرْف. There are no capital letters, but most letters join to the next one, so a letter looks a little different at the start, in the middle or at the end of a word. Six letters, such as alif and dāl, never join to the letter after them.

In everyday writing (newspapers, shop signs, phone messages) the short vowels are usually left out, and readers fill them in from the words they know. Books for children and for learners, like this course, add the short vowels as small marks above and below the letters.

The same script, with a few extra letters, is used for other languages too: Persian in Iran, Urdu in Pakistan and India, Pashto in Afghanistan, Kurdish in parts of Iraq and Iran, and Uyghur in western China. Until 1928 Turkish was also written in Arabic letters. Most of these languages are not related to Arabic, but they took its alphabet, together with many words.

sections.title: Styles of calligraphy

photo.alt: An old parchment page with thick, angular brown-black Arabic letters in Kufic script
photo.caption: A page in Kufic script on parchment (Walters Art Museum, Baltimore).

credit.title: File:Islamic - Folio with Kufic Script - Walters W5522B - Full Page.jpg
credit.author: Anonymous (Islamic)Unknown author

body: Beautiful writing is called خَطّ, a word that also means 'line' and simply 'handwriting'. Over more than a thousand years, calligraphers developed several styles. The oldest well-known one is الْكُوفِيّ, Kufic, named after the city of Kufa in Iraq. It is angular, with straight lines and sharp corners. Early copies of the Qur'an and many old buildings use it.

النَّسْخ, Naskh, is round and very clear. It was the main style for copying books, and most printed Arabic today, in books and newspapers, is based on it. الثُّلُث, Thuluth, is large and elegant, with tall letters and long curves. You see it on mosques, gates and the titles of books.

الدِّيوَانِيّ, Diwani, grew up at the Ottoman court for official letters and decrees; its letters are very round and pressed close together. Finally, الرُّقْعَة, Ruq'a, is a simple, quick style with short strokes. Many people, especially in the eastern Arab world, learn it at school, and their everyday handwriting is a form of Ruq'a.

sections.title: The reed pen and ink

photo.alt: Four reed pens of different sizes, three of them with tips cut at an angle
photo.caption: Reed pens: the tip is cut at an angle with a knife.

credit.title: File:Qalam1.jpg
credit.author: No machine-readable author provided. Baba66 assumed (based on copyright claims).

body: A calligrapher, a خَطَّاط, traditionally writes with a قَلَم, a pen cut from a dried reed, قَصَب. The calligrapher cuts the tip at an angle with a sharp knife and splits it a little so that the ink flows. The width of the tip decides the size of the letters, so a calligrapher keeps many pens. Today قَلَم is also the everyday word for any pen.

The ink, حِبْر, was traditionally made from soot mixed with gum arabic and water, and it is usually black. Calligraphers like smooth paper, and in the past paper was often polished so that the pen could slide easily across it.

Letters have fixed proportions. In many styles the height of the alif is measured in small diamond-shaped dots made with the same pen; this system is linked with Ibn Muqla, a scholar in Baghdad in the 10th century. Students learn by copying a teacher's models for years, and in the Ottoman tradition a student who finished received a licence called an ijāza.

mistakes.why: qalam (pen) is masculine, so 'this' is hādhā, not hādhihi.

sections.title: Writing as art, and the numbers we all use
titleSegs: and the numbers, and the digits

photo.alt: A tiled panel with large blue Arabic letters on white, framed by yellow and blue flower tiles inside a brick arch
photo.caption: Calligraphy in glazed tiles at the Wazir Khan Mosque in Lahore, Pakistan (17th century).

credit.title: File:Arabic Calligraphy at Wazir Khan Mosque.jpg
credit.author: self (Atif Gulzar)

body: In Islamic art, writing became one of the main kinds of decoration. Verses, poems and names are written on mosques, palaces, tiles, pottery, carpets and lamps. From the end of the 7th century many coins of the Islamic world carried only writing and no pictures, and Arabic writing is still on the coins and banknotes of many Arab countries today. On a wall you may see خَطّ made of coloured tiles, like the panel in the photo.

Arabic also has its own digits. In Egypt, Iraq, the Gulf and much of the eastern Arab world, people often write ٠ ١ ٢ ٣ ٤ ٥ ٦ ٧ ٨ ٩. In Arabic these are called الْأَرْقَام الْهِنْدِيَّة, 'the Indian numbers', because the system came from India. In Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia people mostly use 0 1 2 3, which in Arabic are called الْأَرْقَام الْعَرَبِيَّة. A رَقْم is written from left to right, even inside a right-to-left sentence: ٢٨ is 28.

The digits used in English came from India to the Arab world, where scholars such as al-Khwarizmi in Baghdad wrote about them in the 9th century. From there they reached Europe, partly through Spain and North Africa. That is why Europeans call them 'Arabic numerals'.

reading.title: Sami the calligrapher
reading.ar: اِسْمِي سَامِي، وَأَنَا خَطَّاط. أَكْتُبُ بِقَلَمٍ مِنَ الْقَصَب وَبِحِبْرٍ أَسْوَد. أَكْتُبُ مِنَ الْيَمِينِ إِلَى الْيَسَار. فِي الْعَرَبِيَّةِ ثَمَانِيَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ حَرْفًا، وَكُلُّ حَرْفٍ جَمِيل. أُحِبُّ خَطَّ الثُّلُث، لٰكِنْ فِي الْبَيْتِ أَكْتُبُ بِخَطِّ الرُّقْعَة. فِي مَدِينَتِي خَطٌّ جَمِيلٌ عَلَى الْمَسَاجِدِ وَالْبِنَايَاتِ الْقَدِيمَة. الْخَطُّ فَنٌّ قَدِيمٌ وَجَمِيل، وَأَنَا أُحِبُّ عَمَلِي.
reading.en: My name is Sami, and I am a calligrapher. I write with a reed pen and black ink. I write from right to left. Arabic has 28 letters, and every letter is beautiful. I love Thuluth script, but at home I write in Ruq'a. In my city there is beautiful calligraphy on the mosques and the old buildings. Calligraphy is an old and beautiful art, and I love my work.

readingQuestions.prompt: How many letters does Arabic have, according to Sami?
readingQuestions.explain: ثَمَانِيَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ حَرْفًا: eight and twenty, 28 letters.

readingQuestions.prompt: Which style does Sami use at home?
readingQuestions.explain: He loves Thuluth, but at home he writes بِخَطِّ الرُّقْعَة, in Ruq'a.

quiz.prompt: In which direction is Arabic written?
quiz.explain: مِنَ الْيَمِينِ إِلَى الْيَسَار: from right to left.

quiz.prompt: Which style is old and angular, and named after a city in Iraq?
quiz.explain: الْكُوفِيّ is named after Kufa; it has straight lines and sharp corners.

quiz.prompt: Most printed Arabic in books and newspapers is based on which style?
quiz.explain: النَّسْخ is round and clear, the main style for copying books and the base of most print.

quiz.prompt: What is a traditional calligrapher's قَلَم cut from?
quiz.explain: The qalam is cut from a dried reed, قَصَب.

quiz.prompt: Why are the digits 0–9 called 'Arabic numerals' in English?
options: Arabic can only be written with them
They reached Europe through the Arab world
quiz.explain: They came from India to the Arab world, and from there to Europe. In Arabic, ٠ ١ ٢ ٣ are called الْأَرْقَام الْهِنْدِيَّة.

quiz.prompt: Which of these languages is also written in the Arabic script?
quiz.explain: Urdu (Pakistan and India) uses the Arabic script with a few extra letters, like Persian.
